The graph of $y=f(x)$ is shown above. Which of the following could be the graph of $y={f}^{′}(x)?$
questions.worked_solution:
Notice the following:

- At the stationary points, where the tangent line to $y=f(x)$ is parallel to the $x$-axis, we have ${f}^{′}(x)=0.$

- When $f(x)$ is increasing, we have ${f}^{′}(x)>0.$

- When $f(x)$ is decreasing, we have ${f}^{′}(x)<0.$

We can now summarize the information from the graph in the table below. Note that the stationary points were identified (approximately) from the graph of $y=f(x)$:

| $x$ | $(-\infty ,-1)$ | $-1$ | $(-1,0.3)$ | $0.3$ | $(0.3,\infty )$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f$ | $↘$ | $\text{min}$ | $↗$ | $\text{max}$ | $↘$ |
| ${f}^{′}$ | $-$ | $0$ | $+$ | $0$ | $-$ |

Additionally, the function has an inflection point at $x≈-0.3.$ So ${f}^{″}(-0.3)≈0$ and the tangent to the graph of $y={f}^{′}(x)$ must be parallel to the $x$-axis.

We don't know the exact value of ${f}^{′}(-0.3)$ but from the graph of $y=f(x),$ we can conclude that at $x≈-0.3,$ the slope is positive.

Therefore, the graph of $y={f}^{′}(x)$ may look as shown below.

The graph of $y=f(x)$ is shown above. Which of the following could be the graph of $y={f}^{′}(x)$, the derivative of $f(x)?$
questions.worked_solution:
Since the function is piecewise-linear, we get a constant derivative over each linear part.
Notice the following:

- When $f(x)$ is decreasing, we get ${f}^{′}(x)<0.$

- When $f(x)$ is constant, we get ${f}^{′}(x)=0.$

We can now summarize the information from the graph in the table below.

| $x$ | $(-\infty ,4)$ | $4$ | $(4,\infty )$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f$ | $↘$ | $\text{min}$ | $\text{const.}$ |
| ${f}^{′}$ | $-$ | $\text{undef.}$ | $0$ |

From the graph of $y=f(x),$ we can conclude that there are no inflection points. 

Additionally, we have a change of the slope of the tangent line (from negative to $0$) when we pass through $x=4$ from left to right. This means that the derivative is not defined at $x=4$ and we obtain a jump discontinuity at this point for the graph of $y={f}^{′}(x).$

Therefore, the graph of $y={f}^{′}(x)$ may look as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14202834/assets/877fcf017ab91010648de9a375e535ec7697841c8e317196c5759df6aca32e19.png)

The graph of the function $y={f}^{′}(x)$, the derivative of $y=f(x)$, is shown above. Which of the following could be the graph of $y={f}^{″}(x)?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, if we denote $g(x)={f}^{′}(x)$ then ${f}^{″}(x)={g}^{′}(x).$ So, we need to sketch the graph of $y={g}^{′}(x)$ given the graph of $y=g(x),$ as usual.

Notice the following:

- At the stationary points, where the tangent line to $y=g(x)$ is parallel to the $x$-axis, we have ${g}^{′}(x)=0.$

- When $g(x)$ is increasing, we have ${g}^{′}(x)>0.$

- When $g(x)$ is decreasing, we have ${g}^{′}(x)<0.$

We can now summarize the information from the graph in the table below. Note that the stationary points were identified (approximately) from the graph of $y={g}^{′}(x)$:

| $x$ | $(-\infty ,-1)$ | $-1$ | $(-1,0)$ | $0$ | $(0,1)$ | $1$ | $(1,\infty )$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $g$ | $↘$ | $\text{min}$ | $↗$ | $\text{max}$ | $↘$ | $\text{min}$ | $↗$ |
| ${g}^{′}$ | $-$ | $0$ | $+$ | $0$ | $-$ | $0$ | $+$ |

Additionally, the function $y=g(x)$ has inflection points at $x≈-0.5$ and $x≈0.5.$ At the inflection points, we have ${g}^{″}(x)=0,$ so the tangent to the graph of $y={g}^{′}(x)$ must be parallel to the $x$-axis at $x≈-0.5$ and $x≈0.5.$ 

We don't know the exact values of ${g}^{′}(-0.5)$ and ${g}^{′}(0.5)$, but from the graph of $y=g(x)$ we find that the slope of the tangents to ${g}^{′}(x)$ at $x≈-0.5$ and $x≈0.5$ are positive and negative, respectively.  

Therefore, the graph of $y={g}^{′}(x)={f}^{″}(x)$ may look as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14202834/assets/e7791dde88c3f8500047c0ebeb4553055d76a98c0c46f903816f41c1506d6a6a.png)
